text: Comprehensive Analysis of Drosophila Brain Persistent Learning Mechanisms: Neural Circuitry, Synaptic Plasticity, and Molecular Cascades

The central nervous system of Drosophila melanogaster serves as a primary model for deciphering the circuit, cellular, and molecular architecture of persistent learning, memory consolidation, active forgetting, and dynamic behavioral adaptation1. The complete reconstruction of the adult Drosophila central brain connectome—facilitated by high-resolution volume electron microscopy datasets such as Hemibrain and FlyWire—has revealed an intricate network of interconnected neurons, neurotransmitter profiles, and subcellular structures that govern associative learning and cognitive processing1. Understanding how transient sensory experiences are converted into enduring behavioral alterations requires dissecting mechanisms across multiple biological scales: from intracellular second-messenger cascades and local translation to compartmentalized synaptic plasticity, recurrent microcircuit feedback, and central complex navigation networks1.
Connectomic and Architectural Overview of the Persistent Memory Network

The principal center for associative learning and memory consolidation in the Drosophila brain is the mushroom body (MB)1. The MB comprises approximately 2,000 intrinsic neurons per hemisphere, known as Kenyon cells (KCs), whose cell bodies are clustered in the posterior region of the brain10. KC dendrites form a dense input neuropil called the main calyx, which receives predominantly olfactory projection neuron inputs originating in the antennal lobes10. In addition to the main calyx, non-olfactory sensory information enters the MB through specialized accessory calyces: projection neurons from the lobula (LOPNs) and posterior lateral protocerebrum (PLPPNs) project to the dorsal accessory calyx to innervate  KCs, while a parallel visual pathway projecting from the medulla innervates the ventral accessory calyx to contact  KCs13.

The axonal processes of KCs form a tightly bundled tract known as the peduncle, which extends anteriorly before bifurcating into five distinct longitudinal lobes: the medial , , and  lobes, and the vertical  and  lobes10. KCs are classified into three major anatomical and developmental subtypes based on their axonal projections: , , and  KCs. Along the length of these lobes, the parallel KC axon bundles are orthogonally intersected by the presynaptic terminals of approximately 130 dopaminergic neurons (DANs) and the postsynaptic dendritic tufts of 34 mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) divided into 21 distinct cell types10.

The spatial overlap between specific DAN axons and MBON dendrites partitions the MB lobes into 15 anatomically and functionally discrete compartments10. This compartmentalized organization constitutes the core computational architecture of the mushroom body10. DANs originating from the protocerebral posterior lateral 1 (PPL1) cluster predominantly innervate compartments that encode negative valence (aversive reinforcers such as electric shocks), whereas DANs from the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster primarily innervate compartments encoding positive valence (appetitive reinforcers such as sugar rewards)7. The dendrites of MBONs within these compartments sample en passant synapses from thousands of KCs7. Optogenetic activation of individual MBON types demonstrates that they directly drive either behavioral avoidance or approach, establishing that the ensemble output of the MBON network dynamically reflects the net learned valence of a given sensory stimulus7.

These compartmental units are continuously modulated by broadly innervating extrinsic interneurons. A single pair of GABAergic Anterior Paired Lateral (APL) neurons densely innervates the entire MB neuropil, providing global and local feedback inhibition to KCs to maintain sparse odor representations and facilitate reversal learning10. Serotonergic Dorsal Paired Medial (DPM) neurons similarly ramify throughout the lobes to regulate memory consolidation. Connectomic analyses from Hemibrain and FlyWire datasets reveal that beyond feedforward KC-to-MBON transmission, dense axoaxonic and dendrodendritic feedback loops connect MBONs, DANs, and KCs, enabling complex circuit computations such as memory consolidation, state-dependent action selection, reward prediction error calculation, and active forgetting4.
Verification Hierarchy and Evidence Classification
To rigorize the evaluation of persistent learning mechanisms across independent paradigms and methodologies, empirical evidence is categorized into three verification tiers:

Tier 1 (Robust / Replicated): Demonstrated across multiple independent laboratories using convergent methodologies (e.g., live functional calcium/cAMP imaging, cell-type-specific genetic mutants, cell silencing, and connectomic validation).
Tier 2 (Strong / Emerging): Supported by strong mechanistic evidence in targeted paradigms or single high-impact studies, requiring broader replication across diverse behavioral contexts.
Tier 3 (Promising / Theoretical): Computational models constrained by connectomics or emerging biochemical pathways currently undergoing experimental validation in flies.
Systemic Categorization Matrix of Verified Learning Mechanisms

The mechanisms mediating persistent learning, long-term memory storage, active erasure, and sensory-motor transformation in Drosophila are organized below into functional categories, annotated with their evidence tiers.

text: Detailed Mechanistic Analysis across Core Functional Clusters
Presynaptic and Postsynaptic Biochemical Plasticity Cascades

The biochemical basis of associative learning in the mushroom body relies on intracellular coincidence detection executed by type 1 adenylyl cyclase, encoded by the rutabaga (rut) gene21. Sensory cues, such as monomolecular odorants, trigger action potentials in specific subsets of Kenyon cells, inducing calcium inflow through voltage-gated calcium channels and activation of calmodulin10. When an unconditioned stimulus (US)—such as an electric shock or a sugar reward—coincides with odor presentation, reinforcing dopaminergic neurons fire, releasing dopamine onto the corresponding KC axon terminals7. Dopamine binds to G-protein-coupled dopamine receptors, primarily DopR1 (a -coupled receptor), stimulating adenylyl cyclase activity20. The simultaneous presence of calcium/calmodulin and active  subunits produces a synergistic, supra-additive elevation of intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels21. cAMP activates Protein Kinase A (PKA), triggering a downstream phosphorylation cascade that leads to short-term presynaptic functional depression of neurotransmitter release at KC-to-MBON synapses17. Conversely, the cAMP phosphodiesterase encoded by dunce (dnc) degrades cAMP, acting as an enzymatic checkpoint that restricts the temporal window of coincidence and prevents runaway synaptic modification35.

For memory traces to endure over days, local synaptic modifications must be anchored via Synaptic Tagging and Capture (STC)1. Activated KC-to-MBON synapses establish local molecular "tags" immediately after learning1. During subsequent consolidation windows, plasticity-related proteins (PRPs)—synthesized under the control of mTORC1 signaling and nuclear CREB—are selectively captured by these tagged synapses, consolidating local depression or potentiation without non-specifically modifying surrounding inactive terminals1. In addition to heterosynaptic long-term depression (LTD) at KC-MBON synapses, input-timing-dependent plasticity (ITDP) occurs at incoming synapses upstream of or within the calyx22. D2-like dopamine receptors mediate presynaptic modifications that alter the responsiveness of projection neurons to KCs depending on the precise millisecond-level arrival order of sensory and modulatory inputs44. Furthermore, non-canonical cytoskeletal regulation via Rac1 GTPase and Cofilin dynamically alters microfilament assembly within KC axons, controlling both the induction of lability and the physical consolidation of the synapse24.
Recurrent Microcircuit Motifs and Inter-Compartmental Feedback

High-resolution connectomic mapping reveals that mushroom body compartments are not isolated feedforward channels; rather, they are embedded within dense recurrent microcircuits that modulate memory formation, stabilization, and retrieval17. A primary model of circuit-level consolidation operates in the  compartment7. Glutamatergic MBON- neurons receive inputs from  KCs and project directly back to the dendrites of PAM- DANs7. Co-activation of KCs and PAM- DANs depresses the KC-to-MBON- synapse17. Because MBON- provides inhibitory tone to PAM-, depression of MBON- disinhibits PAM- DANs, creating a positive feedforward loop that maintains sustained dopaminergic tone required for long-term memory (LTM) consolidation1.

A distinct oscillatory feedback loop controls memory stabilization in the  compartment14. The MP1 DAN (PPL1-) pairs with MVP2 (MBON-), a GABAergic output neuron2. Following conditioning, MP1 displays enhanced rhythmic calcium oscillations that drive consolidation20. MVP2 expresses two antagonist dopamine receptors: the high-affinity D1-like DAMB receptor and the D2-like  receptor, while MP1 expresses metabotropic  receptors19. Immediately after training, MP1 activity depresses MVP219. After approximately 30 minutes, sequential engagement of DAMB and  activates MVP2, which then releases GABA to bind  on MP119. This negative feedback terminates the post-training oscillatory window of MP1, preventing over-consolidation or non-specific synaptic decay19.

This recurrent architecture is dynamically modulated by internal metabolic state and stress16. Octopaminergic (OA) signals acting through OAMB receptors in the main calyx and heel region integrate arousal and hunger signals to gate appetitive vs aversive memory consolidation10. Furthermore, internal sugar sensors in the central brain evaluate the caloric payload of sugar rewards independently of gustatory taste inputs, directly modulating PAM cluster DAN activity to ensure energy-relevant experiences are preferentially consolidated1. Under chronic stress or aging, dysregulation of neuropeptide F (NPF) and aberrant dopaminergic activity disrupts this gating mechanism, leading to LTM consolidation failure or pathological memory generalization16. Global network normalization is concurrently maintained by the single pair of GABAergic Anterior Paired Lateral (APL) neurons10. Reconstructions using focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) demonstrate that APL forms reciprocal, monosynaptic connections with KCs across all lobe compartments and the calyx3. When a subset of KCs fires in response to an odor, it excites APL, which delivers localized feedback inhibition to surrounding KCs11. This microcircuit decorrelates overlapping odor representations, enforces sparse coding, and is structurally indispensable for visual and olfactory reversal learning3.
Epigenetic Control, De Novo Transcription, and Nuclear Consolidation

The transition from labile short-term memory (STM) and anesthesia-resistant memory (ARM) to long-term memory (LTM) requires nuclear gene transcription and de novo protein synthesis1. This process is governed by cAMP Response Element-Binding Protein (CREB) within  KCs1. Elevated PKA activity phosphorylates dCREB2, converting it into a transcriptional activator that binds to cAMP response elements (CRE) in the promoter regions of target genes1.

Cell-type-specific transcriptomic profiling of mushroom body KCs following LTM acquisition reveals temporally distinct waves of gene expression30. At 1 hour post-induction, a selective transcriptomic burst occurs, upregulating immediate early transcription factors such as Hr38 (an ortholog of mammalian NR4A nuclear receptors) and sr (stripe, an ortholog of Egr1/Arc), alongside genes encoding calcium-dependent exocytosis machinery and cAMP components11. By 24 hours, transcriptomic profiles return to baseline levels, leaving structural synaptic modifications in place11. Emerging evidence links epigenetic chromatin modifications (such as histone acetylation) and post-transcriptional microRNA networks (e.g., miR-137) to the long-term stabilization of these transcriptional programs30.

Circuit-level constraints dictate whether conditioning triggers transcription32. Single training trials or massed training (repeated conditioning without rest intervals) produce short-lasting memory without inducing CREB transcription30. In contrast, spaced training—consisting of multiple conditioning sessions separated by rest intervals—selectively recruits parallel MB microcircuits22. During rest intervals, reduced activity in postsynaptic GABAergic interneurons induces disinhibition of specific dopaminergic neurons, leading to phosphorylated ERK (pERK) accumulation33. This interval-specific disinhibition acts as an internal temporal integrator, ensuring that expensive transcriptional machinery is engaged only when sensory patterns repeat over time22. Circadian clock genes (period, timeless) expressed in small ventral lateral clock neurons (s-LNvs) further gate this transcriptional window, ensuring that memory consolidation efficiency aligns with diurnal physiological rhythms3.
Local Synaptic Translation and Non-Canonical Intercellular Communication

While nuclear transcription supplies necessary molecular building blocks, long-term memory storage requires local synaptic tagging to restrict structural modifications exclusively to activated synapses35. In Drosophila, this local tagging mechanism is mediated by the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding (CPEB) protein Orb235. Orb2 exists in two distinct isoforms: Orb2A and Orb2B38. Orb2A is a short, rapidly degraded protein containing an N-terminal prion-like domain, whereas Orb2B is an abundant, transcript-stabilizing isoform32. Synaptic stimulation induces local translation of Orb2A, which undergoes a conformational change into a self-perpetuating, amyloid-like oligomeric state37.

These Orb2A oligomers act as seeds that recruit Orb2B into stable, insoluble complexes localized specifically to active postsynaptic sites37. Once aggregated, the Orb2 prion-like oligomers unsilence dormant mRNAs—including those encoding Dunce, Rutabaga, and Neurofibromin 1 (Nf1)—driving local protein synthesis that physically stabilizes the modified synapse for days or weeks35. The spatial restriction of this process is further controlled by regulatory elements in the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of orb2 mRNA, which guide the transport and anchoring of transcripts to dendritic spines prior to translation39.

At the intercellular level, a distinct mechanism regulates reward valuation via capsid-mediated RNA transport42. The genes dArc1 and dArc2, derived from Ty3 retrotransposons, encode self-assembling proteins capable of forming virus-like capsids30. These capsids encapsulate dArc1 mRNA and transfer it across extracellular spaces between neurons and glia30. Loss of dArc1/2 capsid assembly causes hyper-sensitivity to low-caloric sugar rewards by disrupting normal signaling in PAM- dopaminergic neurons, revealing that retrotransposon-derived capsid communication acts as a gain control mechanism for reward learning30.
Active Forgetting, Synaptic Erasure, and Homeostatic Maintenance

Memory persistence is governed not only by passive decay, but also by active physiological erasure1. In Drosophila, active forgetting is an ongoing, energy-consuming process managed by specific dopaminergic circuits29. A remarkable feature of this architecture is single-neuron duality: individual dopaminergic neurons, such as PPL1- or MP1, regulate both the acquisition and the subsequent erasure of short-term memory traces43. During conditioning, a high-frequency burst of dopamine from PPL1- activates postsynaptic DopR1 receptors on KCs to induce heterosynaptic LTD20. Following training, the same neuron maintains slow, continuous baseline firing33. This lower concentration of dopamine preferentially engages the DAMB receptor (a -coupled dopamine receptor with high affinity), triggering intracellular signaling via Rac1 GTPase, Scribble scaffold proteins, and Cofilin1. In parallel, D2-like dopamine receptors () expressed on presynaptic DAN terminals (such as the DAN-c1 cluster) act as anti-persistence modulators, suppressing memory holding capacity20.

This pathway progressively reverses the structural and functional synaptic changes induced during learning, actively degrading the memory trace1. However, behavioral forgetting does not always equate to structural erasure1. Unexpressed or "forgotten" memory traces can persist as latent engrams—subthreshold synaptic modifications within KCs—which can be selectively reinstated through optogenetic disinhibition or specific sensory cues1. Active forgetting prevents memory saturation, clears irrelevant environmental associations, and preserves the dynamic range of the mushroom body29.
Sleep-Mediated Memory Reactivation and Homeostatic Plasticity

Sleep plays a direct causal role in consolidating long-term memories in Drosophila3. Following complex conditioning paradigms, such as courtship rejection training or multi-trial associative learning, flies exhibit a homeostatic increase in sleep duration22. During post-learning sleep, dopaminergic neurons that were engaged during acquisition—specifically DAN-aSP13s—undergo dynamic reactivation34. This sleep-dependent reactivation is driven by upstream sleep-promoting neurons and acts on DopR1 receptors expressed in  Kenyon cells ()22. Dorsal Paired Medial (DPM) neurons act as a central hub in this process, releasing serotonin and GABA to link sleep drive directly to KC engram stabilization10. Blocking DAN or DPM reactivation during sleep impairs long-term memory, demonstrating that offline neural replay is necessary to stabilize labile memory traces into permanent storage22.

At the circuit level, sleep consolidation is mediated by a functional push-pull architecture embedded within KC-MBON microcircuits12. Cholinergic MBONs projecting from compartments such as  promote sleep, whereas glutamatergic MBONs projecting from  and  promote wakefulness. Wake-promoting dopaminergic inputs selectively modulate these MBON microcircuits. During prolonged wakefulness, synaptic strength across the mushroom body scales upward, increasing metabolic demand; during sleep, homeostatic down-scaling renormalizes synaptic weights, preserving memory engrams while restoring baseline plasticity3.
Central Complex Navigation, Reinforcement Computations, and System-Level Insights

While the mushroom body evaluates associative valence, the central complex (CX)—comprising the ellipsoid body (EB), protocerebral bridge (PB), fan-shaped body (FB), and lateral accessory lobes (LAL)—serves as the internal navigation and steering center8. Advanced imaging combined with whole-brain connectomics reveals how associative learning interacts with spatial orientation systems35.

In the Ellipsoid Body, visual landmark orientation is maintained by a ring attractor network composed of EPG (Ellipsoid body-Protocerebral bridge-Gall) compass neurons and GABAergic ER (Ellipsoid Ring) neurons45. When an animal navigates a novel visual environment, octopaminergic pathways drive retrograde synaptic plasticity at ER-to-EPG GABAergic synapses35. This plasticity modifies local inhibitory strength, anchoring the internal head-direction "bump" of EPG activity to visual cues without requiring explicit postsynaptic action potentials in EPG cells35. Over extended timescales, population codes across these circuits exhibit representational drift1. While individual KC-MBON active ensembles evolve over time, stable behavioral expression is maintained through redundant, distributed downstream engrams1. Computational models constrained by FlyWire and Hemibrain connectomics demonstrate that multi-compartment dopamine-gated spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) enables continual learning without catastrophic interference9.

Concurrently, reinforcement learning models based on Temporal Difference (TD) algorithms are physically instantiated by PPM3 dopaminergic neurons projecting to the Ellipsoid Body9. In vivo trial-by-trial calcium imaging demonstrates that PPM3 DANs calculate Reward Prediction Error (RPE)47. Initial unpredicted punishments or rewards evoke strong phasic responses in PPM3 neurons47. As pairing with a conditioned visual cue continues, the dopaminergic burst shifts backward in time from the US to the CS47. If an expected US is omitted, PPM3 firing falls below baseline47. PPM3 DANs thus broadcast a dynamic scalar error signal that continuously updates visual-spatial memories47.

Downstream of the CX and MB, steering execution occurs within the Lateral Accessory Lobes (LAL) through a push-pull microcircuit8. Connectomic reconstruction reveals two distinct operational pathways:
The pro-goal pathway recruits PFL2/3 neurons to directly excite descending neurons (DNa01--DNa04), amplifying left-right steering asymmetries to turn the fly toward an appetitive target.
The anti-goal pathway recruits feedforward inhibitory interneurons that invert the pro-goal circuit, overriding goal-seeking behavior to execute rapid escape turns away from aversive obstacles.

Finally, cross-modal structural reweighting provides network flexibility46. Following sensory loss (e.g., blinding or antennae damage), disinhibitory interneurons alter input synaptic fractions in both adult accessory calyces and larval learning centers, expanding remaining sensory pathways into newly vacated synaptic space to preserve adaptive capacity31.
Synthesis of Systems-Level Emerging Principles
Integrating structural connectomics, functional imaging, and molecular genetics reveals several general organization principles governing memory in Drosophila:
High-Dimensional Sparsity to Low-Dimensional Action Vectors

The mushroom body transforms high-dimensional sensory representations into concise behavioral choices7. Thousands of olfactory projection neurons deliver dense, overlapping codes to the calyx. Global feedback inhibition from APL forces KCs into a sparse coding regime where fewer than 5% of KCs fire in response to any single odorant3. This sparse representation projects orthogonally onto the 34 MBONs10. By depressing KC-to-MBON synapses in specific compartments, dopaminergic signaling skews the balance of the MBON ensemble output vector, shifting the fly's behavioral state along an approach-avoidance continuum1.
Temporal Integration via Nested Feedback Scales
The persistence of memory is governed by a cascade of feedback loops operating across different timescales:
Seconds to Minutes: Intracellular cAMP and PKA elevations drive transient presynaptic LTD17.
Minutes to Hours: Recurrent MBON-DAN microcircuits (such as the MBON- / PAM- and MP1 / MVP2 loops) sustain localized activity, triggering pERK activation and CREB-dependent transcription17.
Hours to Days: Local translation of Orb2 forms self-perpetuating prion-like amyloid aggregates that structurally anchor the engram at specific synapses35.
Active Forgetting as Optimal Information Management

Forgetting is not merely passive decay or chemical degradation; it is an active computational process managed by baseline dopaminergic signaling29. By continuously stimulating DAMB and  receptors alongside Rac1/Cofilin cascades, the brain actively erases older or non-reinforced memory traces29. This ongoing erasure maintains dynamic range, prevents network saturation, and ensures flexible behavioral adaptation in changing environments29.
Actionable Experimental and Computational Design Takeaways
When designing causal perturbations or neural network models of insect learning, the following operational principles should be incorporated:

Target Synaptic Amyloid Scaffolding: To selectively eliminate long-term memory while sparing acquisition and short-term expression, target Orb2A oligomerization domains or 3'UTR mRNA regulatory elements rather than upstream cAMP/PKA signaling35.

Include Explicit Internal State Variables: Neural models must incorporate dopamine, octopamine, metabolic sugar sensing, and sleep drive as dynamic modulatory inputs; pure feedforward associative models fail to capture state-dependent consolidation gating7.

Model Active Forgetting as an Engineered Feature: Persistence should be modeled as the net difference between consolidation signals and Rac1/dopamine-driven active erasure, rather than passive weight decay1.

Leverage Cell-Type-Specific Split-GAL4 Driver Lines: Utilize compartment-specific driver lines to manipulate distinct MBON/DAN channels (e.g., separating DopR1 vs DAMB vs  expression) to dissect sub-compartmental consolidation kinetics17.

Account for Offline Consolidation Windows: Experimental paradigms evaluating LTM must account for post-training sleep periods and circadian timing, as interrupting post-learning sleep disrupts offline DAN/DPM replay3.
Strategic Conclusions

Decades of experimental research in Drosophila melanogaster have established a detailed map of the neural and molecular underpinnings of learning and memory1. The classical model of simple linear cAMP/PKA cascades has expanded into an integrated framework involving multi-layered microcircuits, cross-modal structural reweighting, retrotransposon-derived RNA signaling, and temporal difference prediction engines9.
The synthesis of available evidence yields five core conclusions:
Heterosynaptic Long-Term Depression (LTD) at KC-to-MBON synapses, gated by Synaptic Tagging and Capture (STC), serves as the foundational cellular substrate for associative valence assignment7.
Recurrent MBON-DAN microcircuit loops dynamically control the consolidation, gating, and post-training stabilization of memory traces17.
Persistent long-term memory requires nuclear CREB transcription working in concert with localized, prion-like Orb2 amyloid aggregation at individual synaptic terminals30.
Active forgetting, driven by tonic dopaminergic signaling acting through DAMB/ receptors and Rac1/Cofilin pathways, continuously optimizes memory storage capacity29.
Central complex navigation networks seamlessly integrate mushroom body valence outputs with spatial compass representations to execute goal-directed motor decisions35.

As connectomic datasets like FlyWire and Hemibrain continue to be integrated with functional imaging and cell-type transcriptomics, Drosophila remains a primary model for discovering fundamental principles of nervous system function, circuit plasticity, and persistent memory storage1.
